The Painted Desert. A semi-arid badlands region in northeastern Arizona, stretching roughly one hundred miles east to west across the Colorado Plateau. Named for the vivid bands of color in its exposed rock layers—blues, purples, reds, and yellows—it is renowned among geologists for its paleontological deposits and among artists for its dramatic, otherworldly landscape.

The colorful striations come from iron oxide, manganese oxides, and other mineral compounds in sedimentary layers. The colors shift throughout the day with changing light. Adjacent to the Petrified Forest National Park, which contains one of the world's largest deposits of Triassic-era petrified wood, roughly two hundred twenty-five million years old.

Archaeological sites throughout the region contain evidence of ancestral Pueblo and Navajo habitation. The Navajo Nation borders and partially encompasses parts of it. The landscape was shaped by erosion of the Colorado Plateau and lacks significant vegetation. Annual rainfall is typically four to ten inches, making it a semi-arid region rather than a true desert.

The Painted Desert contains important Triassic fossil beds with early dinosaur and synapsid remains. Paleontologists have recovered skeletons of early phytosaurs and primitive mammals. The name Painted Desert was popularized in the early twentieth century by railroad companies and tourism literature highlighting its scenic beauty.

Navajo artisans have long used pigments from the Painted Desert's rocks in traditional weaving and art. The region occupies Arizona's northeastern corner, forming the larger tectonic and geomorphic context known as the Colorado Plateau. The Painted Desert's Triassic fossils speak to early vertebrate history, while the landscape itself testifies to the deep connection between Navajo peoples and this striking, color-stained terrain.
